Systemic Lupus 
Erythematosus
Med Surge Group 16A/9A
Presented by: Gavin Tuosto, Sophie Lipkin, Martin Puthussery, Rachel 
Purnawan, Ayeka Fibleuil, Melina Pedalino, Brianna Mallozzi

• Sex: Females who are 20-40 years of age
• Race & Ethnicity: Higher incidence and 
severity occur in African American, Hispanic, 
Asian, and Indigenous people
• Triggers: Trauma, infection, certain 
medications, UV light exposure, and stress
• Genetics: Family history increases risk
Risk F actors Prevention
The focus is to avoid triggers once 
diagnosed
• Photoprotection: sunscreen, protective 
clothing, avoiding peak daylight UV 
radiation.
• Smoking Cessation: Eliminating tobacco 
use
• Medication Adherence: Taking 
prescribed medication consistently

• Cardiovascular: Exercise and blood 
pressure management
• Diet: A balanced diet rich in omega-3 
fatty acids, antioxidants, and low in 
processed sugars
• Bone Health: Vitamin D and calcium 
supplementation counter the bone 
density loss associated with long-term 
corticosteroid therapies.
Health PromotionEarly Detection
Recognizing early physical warning signs 
and confirming them with diagnostic 
blood tests
• Systemic: Persistent unexplained fatigue, 
low-grade fevers, weight loss.
• Musculoskeletal: Joint pain, stiffness, or 
swelling
• Dermatological: Malar ("butterfly") rash 
across the cheeks and bridge of the nose
• Renal: Edema, hypertension, proteinuria 
(foamy urine)

C l i n i c a l  M a n i f e s t a t i o n s
Neuro:
• Cognitive dysfunction, stroke, psychosis, delirium, peripheral neuropathy
Skin:
• Malar rash, lesions, erythema, warmth, photosensitivity
Eyes:
• Pain, diplopia, proptosis, lid swelling, dryness, grittiness
Musculoskeletal:
• Arthritis, osteoporosis, osteonecrosis
Kidneys:
• Inflammation→hypertension, proteinuria, kidney failure
Chest:
• Pleuritic pain
Pulmonary:
• Pulmonary hypertension, alveolar hemorrhage
Cardiovascular:
• Decreased peripheral pulses, pericarditis, clotting
Low-grade fever, tenderness, infection

Diagnostic T ests
• History , physical exam, blood tests
• ANA: highly sensiti ve screening test
• Anti -dsDNA: highly specifi c, tracks disease 
acti vity
• Anti -Sm: anti body vs. nuclear protein
• C3/C4: complement levels drop in acti ve disease
• CBC: anemia, thrombocytopenia, leuk openia
• ESR/CRP: infl ammati on
• BUN/creati nine/eGFR: kidney functi on
• Urinalysis: proteinuria, hematuria, casts
• Kidney biopsy: confi rms lupus nephriti s
• Anti phospholipid anti bodies: clotti ng risk
Nursing 
Responsibilities
• Skin: erythematous rashes; ask about changes
• Cardiac: auscultate for pericardial fricti on rub
• Lung: abnormal sounds → eff usions/infi ltrati ons
• Musculoskeletal: joint pain, tenderness, warmth, 
sti ff ness, edema
• Neuro: CNS, behavioral, emoti onal changes
• Renal: monitor BP , I&O, edema, foamy urine; follow 
BUN/creati nine
• Eyes: dryness, vision changes; yearly exam 
• Infecti on: monitor temperature; 
immunosuppressants raise risk

Nursing management of SLE should focus on controlling exacerbations, preventing complications, skin protection, educating the 
patient, and providing psychosocial support.
• Monitoring renal function: Assess blood pressure, urine output, edema, BUN, creatinine, and urine protein levels to 
detect early signs of lupus nephritis and prevent kidney damage.
• Monitoring for cardiovascular involvement: Patient at higher risk for cardiovascular disease i.e., hypertension and 
atherosclerosis. Monitor blood pressure, assess for edema, swelling, fever, changes in urine output, and neurological 
changes.
• Protect from UV/sun exposure: Ultraviolet and sun exposure can increase risk of exacerbations. Instruct patient to 
wear sunscreen and appropriate clothing.
• Smoking cessation: Smoking increases risk of respiratory infection, coronary artery disease, and increases blood 
pressure which can worsen kidney function and increase risk of osteoporosis. Patients with SLE at higher risk for lung 
cancer.
• Diet and exercise: Due to risk of osteoporosis from long-term steroid use educate the patient to take calcium and 
vitamin D supplements daily and encourage weight bearing activities to promote bone health.
Medical Management

Medications:
• Antimalarials: Hydroxychloroquine, 
chloroquine
• Corticosteroids: Prednisone, prednisolone
• Monoclonal antibodies: Belimumab
• Immunosuppressants: Methotrexate, 
cyclophosphamide, azathioprine
• NSAIDs: Ibuprofen, aspirin
• Topical steroid: hydrocortisone
• Vitamin D
Medication Manag ement Nursing R esponsibilities 
Nursing Responsibilities:
• Monitor for complications: renal failure, 
cardiovascular disease, infection
• Adequate pain management
• Monitor labs
• Monitor for signs of infection
• Education: avoid UV and sun exposure, 
prevent infection, take frequent rest periods, 
flare recognition and medication adherence
• Psychosocial assessment/support

•Disease Education: Patients with SLE should be educated about the disease pathology, potential organ 
involvement, available educational resources (e.g., brochures), and the importance of medication adherence and 
routine monitoring.
•Lifestyle Modifications: Encourage stress-reduction techniques, good sleep hygiene, regular exercise, and 
participation in emotional support groups. Educate patients on the importance of smoking cessation, as smoking 
can worsen SLE symptoms.
•Dietary Recommendations: Encourage a diet rich in vitamin D and advise patients to avoid alfalfa sprouts and 
echinacea, which may trigger disease activity.
•Photoprotection: Emphasize the importance of avoiding direct sun exposure by scheduling activities 
appropriately, wearing lightweight loose-fitting protective clothing, and using broad-spectrum (UV-A and UV-B) 
sunscreen with an SPF of 30 or higher.
•When to Seek Medical Attention: Report chest pain, sudden weakness or numbness, confusion, severe headache, 
fever, unusual bruising or bleeding, decreased urine output, or bloody urine.
Patient & F amily Education

Discharge Plans
• Maintain regular rheumatology and primary 
care visits
• Complete ordered CBC, kidney function, 
urinalysis, and blood pressure monitoring
• Coordinate referrals to PT, OT, nutrition, or 
mental health services as needed
• Report worsening fatigue, joint pain, rash, 
fever, chest pain, SOB right away
Discharge Planning & Homecare
Homecare
• Maintain regular physical activity as tolerated
• Eat a balanced, heart healthy diet
• Avoid smoking
• Encourage adequate sleep, stress 
management, and emotional/social support
• Stay up to date with recommended vaccines
• Maintain a safe home routine that supports 
independence with ADLs

#1 A 34-year-old female client with SLE is seen in the rheumatology clinic. The patient takes hydroxychloroquine, 
prednisone, and belimumab. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider first?
A.  Bilateral hand stiffness lasting about 30 minutes each morning
B.  Facial erythema across the cheeks that darkens after time outdoors
C.  Painless oral ulcers on the hard palate that began two days ago
D.  Periorbital swelling, foamy urine, and a blood pressure of 158/94 mmHg
#1: Correct answer: D Periorbital edema, foamy urine (proteinuria), and new hypertension together suggest lupus →
nephritis. It affects about 40% of clients with SLE and is a major cause of morbidity and mortality. Early detection 
through serum creatinine and urinalysis allows prompt treatment, which can prevent permanent kidney damage. This is 
the only finding that suggests organ-threatening disease.
Why the other options are incorrect:
Option A: Morning stiffness with joint involvement is expected in SLE, since joint pain and stiffness occur in over 90% of 
clients. It is a common finding to manage, not an urgent one.
Option B: Photosensitive facial erythema is a characteristic skin manifestation. It can flare with sun exposure, and the 
nurse should reinforce sun protection, but it does not signal organ damage.
Option C: Oral ulcers are common and often occur in crops with exacerbations. They can be monitored and treated, 
and they are less urgent than possible kidney involvement.

#2 A client with SLE is starting prednisone. Which statements show the teaching was NOT understood? Select all 
that apply.
A. "I'll wear sunscreen even on cloudy days."
B.   "I'll stop prednisone once my rash clears."
C.   "I'll take calcium and vitamin D daily."
D.   "A fever is probably just my lupus, so I'll rest."
E.   "I'll get a yearly eye exam for my hydroxychloroquine."
#2 Correct answers: B and D
Why they're correct (teaching NOT understood):
B: Corticosteroids must not be stopped abruptly or based on symptoms. Stopping suddenly can cause adrenal 
insufficiency and trigger a flare. 
D: Steroids suppress the immune system, so any fever must be evaluated for infection. Assuming it is lupus delays 
treatment.
Why the others are incorrect (teaching understood):
A: : UV light triggers flares and passes through clouds, so daily protection is appropriate.
C : Long-term steroid use raises osteoporosis and fracture risk. Calcium and vitamin D support bone health.
E: Hydroxychloroquine can cause macular toxicity, so yearly eye exams are essential.
